title: Krishna washes the guests' feet
hookLine: the kings arrive with gifts, everyone gets a job, and Krishna picks the humblest one
last: MARYADA: SOME GROUND YOU DON'T TAKE.

cards: The hall at Indraprastha is crowded. Kings have come from near and far, and none came empty-handed: jewels, fine cloth, horses, gold, things the poem names one after another. Priests tend the sacred fire.

Food goes out by the basketful. And among the guests are the cousins from Hastinapura, Duryodhana and his brothers, not rivals today but family with work to do. After all the planning, the Rajasuya itself is underway.
The question is where each person is standing.

teach.b: A rite this big needs hands, so Yudhishthira hands out jobs. In the telling, the elders Bhishma and Drona watch over everything. Kripa is put in charge of the wealth.
Vidura looks after the spending. Duhshasana sees to the food.
And Duryodhana is given the task of receiving the gifts the kings bring: every jewel and horse meant for his cousin passes through his hands first. Hold onto him; the poem isn't finished with him.
Krishna, the most honored guest, the one so many Hindus worship as God himself, takes a job nobody handed him: washing the feet of the Brahmins who have come. Kneeling, with a basin of water.
That picture is a teaching, and it has a name: seva, service offered as worship. Hinduism doesn't rank jobs the way a palace does. When work is offered to God, the humblest task becomes holy.
You can see it any weekend: people sweeping the temple floor, washing pots in the temple kitchen, lining up shoes at the door, and calling it seva, not chores.
And in a puja, one of the first things offered to the deity is padya, water to wash the feet, the welcome you'd give an honored guest.
Krishna is on both sides of that bowl: worshiped with it, and holding it. So the small job, the one nobody sees, still counts. And not every king in the hall is happy about who's being honored.
One of them is about to say so out loud.

how: Seva, service offered as worship, is a living Hindu practice: volunteers clean temples, cook and serve in temple kitchens and look after guests, and in puja the deity is welcomed with water for the feet (padya) like an honored guest. Some retellings of the Sabha Parva hold up Krishna washing the Brahmins' feet at the Rajasuya as a picture of it.

o: a palace hall built by a great asura builder
a yearly harvest feast given for a whole city
a royal rite where kings honor one king with gifts

games.q: jobs at the Rajasuya — tap the pairs.
p: washed the feet of the Brahmins

s: seva means a job you get paid to do at the temple
seva is service offered as worship, freely given, and the job doesn't have to be grand.
Duryodhana was given the job of receiving the gifts
the wealth meant for his cousin passed through his hands first.
Krishna sat apart as a guest of honor and did no work
the poem says he chose to wash the feet of the Brahmins.

games.q: you're Krishna, the honored friend at Yudhishthira's great rite. there's a job for everyone. which do you take?
o: wash the feet of the Brahmins.
sit beside the king and greet the guests.
games.why: the poem says Krishna chose to wash the feet of the Brahmins who had come: seva, the humblest job offered as worship.

practice: Bring to mind one small job waiting for you today: the dishes, a ride for someone, a message a friend needs. Picture doing it slowly and well, the way Krishna held the basin.
Many Hindus offer their work with a quiet phrase, Krishnarpanam, to Krishna I offer this. If you pray, offer that job the same way; if not, simply decide to do it with care, as a gift.

wordCard.voice: The Rajasuya. A royal consecration where kings bring gifts to recognize one sovereign, and where Krishna, the guest of honor, chose to serve.

orig.note: Sanskrit rājasūya: the royal consecration rite Yudhishthira performs at Indraprastha.

carryVoice: Your line: seva: serving others is worship. Krishna knelt with the basin. Day seven hundred fifty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Rajasuyika Parva (the rite performed; jobs assigned to the Kurus; Krishna washes the Brahmins' feet)
